summary: Defines MIB objects for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs), and extends earlier work to cover 10 gigabit per second MAUs. It obsoletes RFC 1515 and RFC 2668. It is a proposed standard that has been replaced by RFC 4836.

eli5.summary: A MAU is the part that plugs a device into the Ethernet wire. This lists the gauges a manager can read on it, including for very fast links. RFC 4836 has since replaced it.

subtitle: The SNMP objects a network manager reads and sets to monitor Ethernet medium attachment units, now covering 10 Gb/s links.

tldr.problem: Ethernet keeps gaining new speeds and cable types, and network managers need a standard way to see and control the Medium Attachment Unit (MAU) on each port or repeater.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3636 defines an SMIv2 MIB module that maps the IEEE 802.3 MAU management objects onto SNMP objects, and extends the earlier RFC 2668 module with 10 gigabit per second MAU types and a 64-bit false-carrier counter.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 1515 and RFC 2668, and it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4836.

facts.value: IEEE Std 802.3, 2002 edition, as amended by 802.3ae-2002

today: RFC 3636 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4836, so new work should use that document. It obsoleted RFC 2668 and RFC 1515.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3636 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs). It contains one MIB module, which extends the module in the earlier RFC 2668.

The RFC says plainly that Ethernet keeps evolving, with faster speeds, new cabling and new features, and that this evolution may require changes to the managed objects. It treats itself as a snapshot of one stage: later revisions or new documents may follow.

The module is written for the Internet-Standard Management Framework. MIB objects are generally reached through SNMP and are defined with the Structure of Management Information, here SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).
sections.eli5: Ethernet gets faster and gets new plugs every few years. This memo lists the gauges for the plug part, and it says the list may need to grow again later.

sections.title: Repeater MAUs and Interface MAUs
sections.content:
The objects describe attributes of an IEEE 802.3 MAU. The IEEE 802.3 CSMA/CD standard defines several MAU types. A MAU may be connected to an IEEE 802.3 repeater or to an 802.3 (Ethernet-like) interface, so the RFC calls them repeater MAUs and interface MAUs.

The definitions are based on Section 30.5 (layer management for 10 Mb/s, 100 Mb/s, 1000 Mb/s and 10 Gb/s MAUs), Section 30.6 (management for link auto-negotiation) and Annex 30A of IEEE Std 802.3, 2002 edition, as amended by IEEE Std 802.3ae-2002.

A MAU can also be internal, with its functionality implemented entirely inside a device. A managed repeater may, for example, contain an internal MAU through which management traffic reaches its agent. Internal MAUs may or may not be managed. If they are, their objects belong in dot3RpMauBasicGroup (repeater MAUs) or dot3IfMauBasicGroup (interface MAUs).
sections.eli5: Some plug parts sit on a hub that copies traffic to many ports, and some sit on a single network card. Some plug parts are hidden inside the device itself. The list has gauges for all of these.

sections.title: Lineage and Companion MIBs
sections.content:
This MIB is meant to be a superset of RFC 2668: it includes every object from that module, with new and updated definitions. Implementors are encouraged to support all applicable conformance groups. The chain goes back through RFC 2239 to RFC 1515, and each step kept the older objects and added new ones.

An agent is assumed to implement at least the system group of the SNMPv2 MIB. The interface-MAU objects extend the Interfaces MIB (RFC 2863): an agent that implements them MUST also implement the relevant groups of ifCompliance3, and ifMauIfIndex carries the same value as the ifIndex of the interface the MAU is connected to. The agent is also REQUIRED to comply fully with dot3Compliance2 of the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB (RFC 3635).

When the objects manage a 10GBASE-W PHY, the agent MUST also support the Ethernet WAN Interface Sublayer MIB (RFC 3637) and follow its interface layering model. Repeater-MAU objects extend the 802.3 Repeater MIB (RFC 2108), and their rpMauGroupIndex and rpMauPortIndex values SHALL equal the rptrPortGroupIndex and rptrPortIndex of the port the MAU is attached to.
sections.eli5: Each new edition of this list keeps all the old gauges and adds new ones. The new list also has to agree with the lists for network cards and hubs, so that the same port has the same number everywhere.

sections.title: What the MIB Module Defines
sections.content:
The module lives under snmpDot3MauMgt, which is { mib-2 26 }. It defines a JackType textual convention (values from other(1) to fiberLC(14)), a set of OBJECT-IDENTITY values naming each MAU type under dot3MauType, and tables for repeater MAUs, interface MAUs, auto-negotiation, jacks and broadband MAUs.

The interface table ifMauTable is indexed by ifMauIfIndex and ifMauIndex. Its objects include ifMauType (the operational MAU type, or the object identifier { 0 0 } when unknown), ifMauStatus (a read-write administrative state), ifMauMediaAvailable, jabber state and counters, ifMauFalseCarriers and ifMauDefaultType. When auto-negotiation is off or not implemented, setting ifMauDefaultType forces the MAU into the new operating mode.

The auto-negotiation table adds ifMauAutoNegAdminStatus, ifMauAutoNegConfig and capability objects for what the local MAU supports, advertises and has received. The older integer capability object is deprecated in favour of the ...Bits objects.

Section 3.6 maps IEEE 802.3 managed objects (for example aMAUType and aJabber) to the matching SNMP objects. Two groups were left out: aIdleErrorCount, only useful for 100BaseT2, which is not widely implemented, and the selector-ability objects, needed only for isoethernet (802.9a).

For 10 Gb/s, the module adds MAU type identities such as dot3MauType10GigBaseX, 10GigBaseLX4, 10GigBaseR, 10GigBaseER, 10GigBaseLR, 10GigBaseSR, 10GigBaseW, 10GigBaseEW, 10GigBaseLW and 10GigBaseSW.
sections.eli5: For each plug part there is a row of gauges: what kind of plug it is, whether it is on or off, whether a cable is really there, and how many odd signals it saw. A manager can read them, and a few can be changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several objects have a MAX-ACCESS of read-write, and setting them can seriously affect the network. The RFC lists enabling or disabling a MAU, changing a MAU's default type, enabling, disabling or restarting auto-negotiation, and changing the capabilities a MAU advertises during auto-negotiation.

Readable objects may be sensitive too, because it may be undesirable to let unauthorized parties see statistics or status for individual links. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC recommends considering the SNMPv3 security features, says that deploying SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED, and makes it the customer or operator's responsibility to configure access so that only legitimate principals can GET or SET these objects.
sections.eli5: Some of the dials can switch a port off, so only the right people should be allowed to turn them. Even reading the gauges can tell strangers things you want kept private.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2668
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the changes made to RFC 2668. The IEEE 802.3 references were updated to the 2002 edition and IEEE 802.3ae was added. Object identities were added for the 10 gigabit MAU types, and ifMauTypeListBits was extended with bits for them.

The ifMauMediaAvailable description was updated for 10 Gb/s behaviour, with new enumerations such as pmdLinkFault, wisFrameLoss, wisSignalLoss, pcsLinkFault, excessiveBER, dxsLinkFault and pxsLinkFault. A 64-bit ifMauHCFalseCarriers counter was added, with updated compliance statements, and the mapping to IEEE managed objects was added as a new section.
sections.eli5: This edition added gauges for the newest, fastest Ethernet and a bigger counter that does not run out quickly on fast links.

cells: 100 Mb/s devices, auto-negotiation on interface MAUs, jack management

items.label: other
items.desc: The MAU is in a state other than 2 through 6.

items.label: unknown
items.desc: True state is unknown, for example while initializing.

items.label: standby
items.desc: Forces DI and CI to idle; applies only to link type MAUs.

items.label: shutdown
items.desc: Behaves as if powered down or not connected.

items.label: reset
items.desc: Resets the MAU like a power-off, power-on cycle of at least one-half second.
